lesson.title: 32 Calques Deep-Dive
lesson.subtitle: The curated compound gallery — Kühlschrank to Kummerspeck — with literal glosses

hook.title: The Gallery
hook.content: The compendium keeps thirty-two curated compounds, each one a two-word philosophy lesson. Kühlschrank: cool-cabinet (the fridge). Kummerspeck: grief-bacon (comfort-eating weight). Glühbirne: glowing-pear (a light bulb). Backpfeife: cheek-whistle (a slap so hard the cheek rings). Wissenschaft: knowledge-ship (science). German translated the Latin science words into native Lego — perceptio became Wahrnehmung ('truth-taking'), conceptus became Begriff ('by-grip'). This lesson walks the gallery and teaches you to read every frame.

footnotes.title: Why Calques Matter
footnotes.content: A calque is a loan-translation: borrow the MEANING, build it from your OWN parts. Fernseher calques tele-vision (far-seeing) from Greek and Latin roots — the same idea, Germanic wood. English borrowed the Greek boards instead; that is why 'television' sounds smart and 'Fernseher' sounds like furniture.

pattern.title: Read the Frames
pattern.content: The household row: Krankenhaus (sick-house), Krankenschwester (sick-sister, a nurse), Staubsauger (dust-sucker), Flugzeug (flight-stuff), Feuerzeug (fire-stuff), Fahrzeug (drive-stuff), Spielzeug (play-stuff), Werkzeug (work-stuff) — the -zeug family alone is a toolbox. The body row: Zahnarzt (tooth-doctor), Fingerhut (finger-hat, a thimble), Glühbirne (glowing-pear). The city row: Spätkauf (late-buy, the Berlin corner store), Autobahn (car-track), Eisenbahn (iron-track). The time row: Donnerstag (thunder-day), übermorgen (over-morrow), vorgestern (before-yesterday). Each one is an app in two words.
pattern.linguist_note: The -zeug family (das) and the -er agent family (der) are gender laws doing double duty as compound factories — the suffix court from the Gender lesson runs the gallery's grammar.

exercises.prompt: Gallery wall one — match the compound with its literal gloss:
exercises.target_answer: der Kühlschrank, das Krankenhaus, die Glühbirne, der Kindergarten, der Fußball, der Regenbogen, das Heimweh
exercises.meaning: refrigerator, hospital, lightbulb, kindergarten, football, rainbow, homesickness
exercises.explanation: Read the parts, get the meaning free — and note the head word donating each gender. Fußball, Regenbogen and Heimweh are English's own compounds seen in the German mirror.

exercises.prompt: The -zeug family: why is the lighter 'das Feuerzeug'?
options: Fire is neuter in German culture
All -zeug compounds are neuter — das is the suffix law
exercises.target_answer: All -zeug compounds are neuter — das is the suffix law
exercises.meaning: das Feuerzeug, das Flugzeug, das Spielzeug
exercises.explanation: One suffix, one gender, a whole toolbox of machines: flight-stuff, fire-stuff, play-stuff. And the picnic verdict rides the same reading habit: der Kuchen schmeckt — taste's cousin smack at work.

exercises.prompt: 'Fernseher' is the calque of which English word (built from Greek tele + Latin vision)?
exercises.explanation: Same Greek-Latin idea, Germanic wood: fern (far) + Seher (seer). A loan-translation — a calque.

exercises.prompt: 'Kummerspeck' — grief-bacon — means what in real usage?
options: Weight gained from comfort eating during emotional stress
exercises.target_answer: Weight gained from comfort eating during emotional stress
exercises.explanation: German welds two concrete nouns into an entire human situation — the compounding system as emotional vocabulary.

exercises.prompt: Say in German: "The children play in the kindergarten"
exercises.meaning: The children play in the kindergarten

vocab_hints.note: das Spiel (the game) + -en — Spielzeug is play-stuff
in + dem — the same contraction from the Hidden Twins lesson

exercises.explanation: The compound explains itself in context: Kinder + Garten — and English borrowed the whole word intact in 1840.
exercises.idea: The children play in the kindergarten
cues: Start with "Die" and anchor "Kinder" in position 2.

summary.outcome: Read and gloss the 32 curated calques, including the -zeug family.

use_example.english: The children play in the kindergarten.

summary.takeaway: Every calque is a loan-translation — tele-vision became far-seer; read the Germanic wood instead of the Greek boards.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: Compound Builder Workshop — assemble compounds from taught nouns and predict the gender.

haus.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *hūsą — an exact twin of English house, down to the diphthong. [wiktionary]

kind.context_translation: The child plays in the garden.
kind.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *kindą, related to the root of English kin — 'of the family'. The t → z shift never fired here; the d hardened to t instead. [wiktionary]

garten.context_translation: The children play in the garden.

zeit.etymology_derivation: t → z [ts] (cognate with English "tide", as in Yuletide or time and tide).

fußball.etymology_derivation: Fuß + Ball — a calque of English football; Fuß is foot with the t→s shift. [wiktionary]

regenbogen.context_phrase: Nach dem Regen sehen wir einen Regenbogen.
regenbogen.context_translation: After the rain we see a rainbow.
regenbogen.etymology_derivation: Regen (rain) plus Bogen (bow — twin of English bow); the page lists English rainbow as the parallel cognate — the exact same compound. [wiktionary]

heimweh.context_phrase: Nach einer Woche hatte sie Heimweh.
heimweh.context_translation: After a week she was homesick.
heimweh.etymology_derivation: Heim (home, Proto-Germanic *haimaz) + Weh (pain, from the root behind English woe): home-woe, homesickness. [wiktionary]

zahnarzt.context_translation: The dentist looks at my teeth.
zahnarzt.etymology_derivation: Zahn (tooth) + Arzt (doctor) - literally tooth-doctor; Zahn shows the t-to-z shift from the same ancient root as English tooth (PIE *h₃dónts). [wiktionary]

hauptstadt.context_phrase: Berlin ist die Hauptstadt von Deutschland.
hauptstadt.context_translation: Berlin is the capital of Germany.
hauptstadt.etymology_derivation: Haupt + Stadt, literally head city; the page traces Haupt to the PIE head root that also yields Latin caput, so English capital is the Latin twin, and Stadt is the twin of English stead. [wiktionary]

schmecken.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *smakkijan — Wiktionary: 'Compare English smack and smatch'. [wiktionary]

ruhig.etymology_derivation: From Ruhe 'rest, calm' + -ig; Middle High German ruowec meant quiet. [wiktionary]

rippe.context_phrase: Er hat sich eine Rippe gebrochen.
rippe.etymology_derivation: From Old High German rippa, from Proto-Germanic *ribją meaning rib, reef. English rib is a listed cognate. [wiktionary]

während.etymology_derivation: Originally the present participle of währen (to last — the page traces it to PIE *h₂wes-, the root of English was), later rebracketed into a preposition; English during and while are unrelated. [wiktionary]

enkelkind.context_translation: The grandchild is playing in the garden.
enkelkind.etymology_derivation: Enkel plus Kind; Enkel has no living English cognate, while Kind goes back to Proto-Indo-European genh1, the root of archaic English kin. [wiktionary]

th_to_d.name: The Dental Shift (TH → D)
th_to_d.historical_linguistics: Every single original Germanic "th" sound systematically shifted to "d" in High German, while English kept the ancient "th".
th_to_d.philological_note: Around 500–700 AD in the High German Consonant Shift, dental fricatives hardened into voiced dental stops.

d_to_t.name: The Stop Shift (D → T)
d_to_t.historical_linguistics: Where English kept Germanic "d", High German hardened it into "t".
d_to_t.philological_note: Voiced stops became voiceless. Explains pairs like day ↔ Tag, door ↔ Tür, and drink ↔ trinken.
d_to_t.literature_source: Complementary to the TH → D shift: as TH took over D, original D shifted to T in High German.

p_to_pf_f.name: The Labial Shift (P → PF / F)
p_to_pf_f.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /p/ shifted to the affricate "pf" at the beginning of words, and to "f" or "ff" after vowels.
p_to_pf_f.philological_note: Explains apple ↔ Apfel, pepper ↔ Pfeffer, hope ↔ hoffen, and sleep ↔ schlafen.

t_to_s_ss_z.name: The Sibilant Shift (T → S / SS / Z)
t_to_s_ss_z.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /t/ shifted to sibilant "s/ss/ß" after vowels, and to "z" (/ts/) at the beginning of words.
t_to_s_ss_z.philological_note: Reveals water ↔ Wasser, eat ↔ essen, better ↔ besser, two ↔ zwei, and to ↔ zu.
t_to_s_ss_z.literature_source: Walter Skeat - Primary dental affrication and spirantization

k_to_ch.name: The Velar Shift (K → CH)
k_to_ch.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /k/ softened to the fricative "ch" in medial and final positions.
k_to_ch.philological_note: The Ach-Laut [x] occurs after a, o, u; the Ich-Laut [ç] occurs after e, i, ä, ö, ü.

v_to_b.name: The Bilabial Shift (V / F → B)
v_to_b.historical_linguistics: Intervocalic /v/ and /f/ in English regularly correspond to voiced /b/ in German.
v_to_b.philological_note: Explains give ↔ geben, live ↔ leben, love ↔ lieben, over ↔ über, and seven ↔ sieben.
v_to_b.literature_source: Proto-Germanic bilabial spirant closing to stop in High German

y_gh_to_g_ch.name: The Palatal & Guttural Link (Y → G & GH → CH)
y_gh_to_g_ch.historical_linguistics: English vocalized palatal "g" into "y" (say, day, yesterday) and silenced "gh" (night, laugh, light). German preserved them as "g" or "ch".
y_gh_to_g_ch.philological_note: Explains why English spelling has silent 'gh' letters — they were original German-like gutturals!

latin_ieren.name: The Latin / Romance Layer (-ate / -ize → -ieren)
latin_ieren.phonetic_rule: English verbs ending in -ate, -ize, -ify, -ish ➔ German verbs ending in -ieren
latin_ieren.historical_linguistics: English verbs derived from Latin or French directly map to German verbs ending in -ieren.
latin_ieren.philological_note: Past participles of -ieren verbs never take the "ge-" prefix (studieren → studiert).
latin_ieren.literature_source: Middle High German productive loan suffix from Old French -ier

strong_verbs_ablaut.name: The 7 Strong Verb Classes (Ablaut)
strong_verbs_ablaut.phonetic_rule: English irregular strong verbs with internal vowel changes ➔ German strong verbs following the exact same Ablautreihe
strong_verbs_ablaut.historical_linguistics: Shared 7 Proto-Germanic verb classes where tenses are formed by shifting root vowels.
